claims.text: A framework coupling high-throughput first-principles phonon simulations with machine-learning regressors can accurately identify HEAs with very low phonon thermal conductivity.
The machine-learning regressors capture chemical disorder and local structural effects.
The proposed framework will outperform standard first-principles or semi-empirical methods by at least 15–20% in predictive accuracy.
The intended materials are multi-principal-element HEAs in as-synthesized or conventionally processed single-phase or near-single-phase solid-solution states.
The pipeline will be trained on aggregated experimental and computed phonon-scattering data.
The trained pipeline will screen large numbers of HEA compositions for low thermal conductivity.
Moderate to high temperatures are representative of typical thermal-insulation operating regimes.
Local chemical fluctuations, mass and bond distortions, and multicomponent disorder in HEAs enhance phonon scattering.
Atomic-size mismatch, mass variance, bond electronegativities, and partial phonon densities of states are disorder-sensitive descriptors relevant to phonon scattering.
Using those descriptors enables the model to capture subtle phonon-scattering routes and accurately predict low thermal conductivity.
The approach will reduce mean absolute error by at least 15–20% relative to conventional methods.
The approach will identify HEA candidates with thermal conductivity below 1 W/(m·K).
Traditional first-principles and semi-empirical estimates do not fully account for multielement disorder in HEAs.
The approach is applicable only to solid-solution-dominated HEAs with minimal second-phase formation.
Performance outside the training-composition range or for extensively phase-segregated alloys is uncertain.
Accuracy gains for compositionally complex or sparsely sampled systems cannot be guaranteed without additional experimental data.
The benchmark will test quaternary-to-senary HEAs and measure phonon thermal conductivity across elevated temperatures.
X-ray diffraction will be used to verify that tested alloys are single-phase or near-single-phase.
The hypothesis is falsified if more than half of tested compositions deviate from model predictions by over 20% across the measured temperature range.
